rationale: Describes a chamber where a lifetime passes in a few hours; the simulated-world idea gestures at VR but time compression and no mechanism for the senses are given.
A sun-powered ball that rolls after a child is a loosely pet-like toy; the 1962 toy dog was a leash-steered animal imitation, a different mechanism.
Household robots fitted with sound sensors keyed to names and simple spoken commands match voice-command recognition; the context is domestic robots rather than a portable computer.
A surgically implanted cybrain that computes tactics is an implant extending ability, but a cochlear implant restores hearing, a different function.
Robot lenses that record what they see for masters hint at remote sight, but the quote describes recording, not live operation of a manipulator.
A satchel plugged into a computer outlet in a hospital suggests networked medical computing, but nothing about records or diagnosis appears in the quote.
A machine mind with electronic memory stacks points loosely at electronic computing; Colossus was a code-breaking machine, and the quote states no calculation function.
An automaton acting independently in response to its sensitive organs points toward machine senses, but the quote is about autonomy, not sensors surpassing human senses.
Programs punched by men that run a ship matches onboard computer control of a vehicle in function; the quote gives no detail on orbit calculation.
A multiple-calculator appearing in a room is a vague calculating device; no programmability, electronics or code-breaking function is stated.
A computer digesting factors to produce a spacecraft's origin and trajectory matches navigation calculation; the thought-driven input is a different mechanism.
A cyborg brain acting as a calculator is a body-augmentation notion, but the real cochlear implant restores a sense, so the function differs.
A table governed by radio from a person's brain impulses matches brain-to-device control in function; the real system was an implant driving a cursor.
A cap that reads a visualized world and shows it on a screen is brain-signal-to-machine control in function; the mechanism is vague and the real device moved a cursor.
A clerk calling up lists of records on a screen matches quick electronic lookup in function; the quote gives no query or large-collection mechanism.
Future people extracting a full story from unconscious visitors' memories matches reading memories from the brain; the real 2008 work reconstructed simple viewed images.
A computer combining probable fathers and mothers pairs people by recorded traits, loosely like dating matching, but the purpose is breeding rather than partnership.
A chess machine being entered into the qualifying tournament matches computer chess aimed at human-level play; the quote has no mechanism, and the milestone is a consumer product.
An electronic brain and autopilot steering a spaceship from a course tape matches onboard guidance in function; details of calculation are thin.

Searching hundreds of millions of archive cards to find information on a planet matches large-collection retrieval; the days-long, librarian-staffed process differs from seconds-long interactive queries.
A library view-screen with index buttons giving instant access to legal text matches interactive online retrieval; the portable pinhead-tape medium differs.
Calculators linked to copiers that automatically produce texts match machine-generated writing in function; the real FoG generated forecasts from data, and the mechanism here is vague.
A computer weighing genetics and stress to forecast violence is predictive in spirit, but the milestone is a database of wanted persons, not prediction.
A dicto-typer that turns dictation into typed text matches the function of dictation transcription; no recognition mechanism is stated and it is already in common use.
An electrical machine doing mathematics beyond the human brain is evocative of computing but names no programmability, storage or data processing.
A robot's flat, inflectionless but intelligible speech matches artificial voice output in function; the mechanism is not described.
Computer storage and recall of vast knowledge matches large-scale retrieval in function; the quote says nothing about query-based search.
A computer answering aloud with a proverb through a Voder-like voice matches synthesized speech in function; the passage is about a spoken reply, not how it is generated.
Books answering spoken questions with a precise location match a system that answers questions in ordinary language; it directs to a plan rather than giving broad factual answers.
Presenting an identity disc to a machine that hums, clicks and opens a gate matches a machine-read token granting access; the disc's form and gate context differ from a punched dining-hall card.
Computers ranking reports of murders to find a fugitive point loosely at police data analysis; the quote does not say how, and the milestone is a national records database.
Thinking and having machines respond matches thought-driven control of devices in function; the keyboard and transport effects differ from a cursor implant.
A Minicalculator used by health statisticians is a small calculating device for personal use; the quote gives no power or portability detail.
Pressing an identifying wristband to a lock-face matches a machine-read token opening a door; the wearable form and clothing dispenser add differences.
An Elecalc plotting jump courses in a ship's computing room matches navigation calculation in function; the interstellar context and no mechanism differ.
A robot that points technologists to records and obeys simple directions is loosely retrieval-related, but the quote centres on a robot helper rather than a searchable store.
A character mentally commanding a robot matches thought control of a machine; the mechanism is unspecified and the real case was an implanted cursor.
Computers handling an almost unlimited number of variables for astronomical calculation match scientific computing; the quote has no speed or machine detail.
Silver probes plunged into wrist nerves connecting an operator to a computer match a neural interface; the nerves are peripheral, not brain signals driving a cursor.
An assembly line inspecting a car every fifteen minutes evokes automated manufacturing, but it is inspection with workers, not a self-running plant.
A stylus tracing a glowing line on a wall hints at a writable luminous surface, but nothing says the image is erasable or rewritable like paper.
An electromechanical device educating a six-year-old to an adult level matches machine-delivered instruction in function; how it teaches, tests or grades is not described.
An automatic electronic scanner guard that lets a person pass as an employee matches machine-checked identity access; the quote does not say what token is read.
Shuttled magnetic elements carrying instrument data and commands to a robot ship evoke remote control, but the human does not see or feel through sensors in the quote.
A beam that reveals a visitor's identity and purpose from a distance is identification at a glance, but nothing says faces or stored images are matched.
Inserting pass cards into the mouth slot of an automatic gate guard matches a machine reading a card for entry; the dystopian city setting differs from a dining hall.
A vast space-chart above the deck suggests a navigation display, but the quote shows nothing about live positions or computer-driven tracking.
A character struck by how real a hallucination feels evokes convincing simulated experience, but no machine feeding the senses is described.
A librarian submitting foreign literature to analysis for idea-content gestures at machine handling of documents, but it is analysis, not query-based finding.
A pre-recorded tape from the course computer driving the autopilot matches computer-computed courses steering a ship; the tape-fed form differs from an onboard orbital computer.
People speaking name, number and rating into a machine that returns an address disc matches spoken input to a machine; it is dictated data entry, not recognition of command words.
Equipment centrally registered with a built-in signal summoning repair machinery is household automation in spirit, but it concerns maintenance, not a home responding to occupants.
A camera feeding a central police computer that matches a description and alerts robots matches face matching against stored data; robot police and a description file differ.
Tracking saucers feeding data to computers that return guidance matches computing spacecraft courses; the computing is ground-based rather than onboard.
A Calculator that knows people's emotional make-up and picks pairings matches matching by recorded traits; the aim is a gifted child, not romantic partnership.
A global index classed by thumb and finger marks anticipates fingerprint identification, but it is a manual classified index, not automatic reading or matching.
Fully automatic factories making spare parts to make a machine self-sufficient match an unstaffed plant in function; the quote gives no mechanism.
A machine remotely connected to one's mind matches thought-driven control in function, with no interface mechanism described.
Hurling thought-waves into a machine brain evokes mind-to-machine links, but it is training the machine, not using brain signals to control it, and it fails.
An android with a built-in recorder reporting on children's dreams matches covert recording for state surveillance; ECHELON worked by automated interception and keyword screening.
A cybernetic control system installed to prevent reactor accidents points toward automated plant control, but it is a safety interlock, not a self-running plant.
Robots normally mediated by area computers matches a central computer directing many robots; the quote's twist about controlling them directly differs from warehouse robot fleets.
A machine announcing a well-modulated spoken description matches artificial voice output; how the voice is produced is not described.
Feeding a heading to a robot mount through a brain link matches thought-based control of a machine; the real case controlled a cursor via implanted electrodes.
Punch-card formulas fed to calculators to produce articles and stories match automatic text generation by formula; the real FoG generated forecasts from live data.
A silvery telechart indispensable for navigation suggests a plotting display, but no live tracking or computer is described in the quote.
A robot set for profession and ability that finds a person matches retrieval from a database; the steno-robot adds dictation, and no speed or scale is stated.
Circuits reading lips and producing sound patterns match machine-generated speech in function; the lipreading input is a different mechanism.
A chest strap sensing a viewer's lean to pick plot branches is body sensing controlling a machine, but not touch or gesture on a screen.
A machine that weighs all stored information to answer coded problems matches a general question answerer; questions are coded, not put in ordinary language.
Robots dispatched when scanning fails say nothing about recognising speech or voice commands.
A Voteplate fed into a guide-robot's chest slot matches a card machine-read to authenticate its holder; the commanding of robots is a different context.
Calling up survey data for a named star system by button matches record lookup; the quote shows only a reply, not a large collection searched.
A vast man-made brain costing hundreds of millions evokes brain-like computing, but the quote has no interconnected units or learning.
A film chart in which the eye sees an actual wedge of space matches a volumetric view in function; it is a stereoscopic film device rather than a hologram.
Fingerprint and retinal patterns used for checking identity match biometric identification; the quote names no automatic reading or file matching.
A probe that would extract an agent's memories directly matches reading memories from a brain; the real work only reconstructed simple viewed images.
A portable scriptwriter carried in a case suggests a text-composing machine, but nothing says it generates text itself.
A device copying a person into a lifelike android matches a robot double in function; Disney's Lincoln was a scripted animatronic with no neural copying.
Machines deep-probing a mind to extract what a person has thought about match thought-reading in function; the real 2008 system recovered only simple viewed images.
Fast circuits scanning storage tubes for one person's record match electronic record search; the genetic-records context and tube storage differ from a bibliographic database.
Ship computers ticking to keep a spacecraft on course match onboard computers guiding a craft; the interplanetary context is broader than orbital maneuvers.
A mind-probe used in trials to extract truth, and found foolable, matches reading thoughts from a brain in function; there is no mechanism, and the real system reconstructs images.
A psycho-search that scans minds, dodged by a false brain pattern, matches mind-reading in function; the passage gives no mechanism.
Microscopic crystalline relays packed by the million into a few cubic inches match solid-state miniaturisation; the quote calls them relays rather than transistors or chips.
A World Brain whose plastic creations act under it matches a central computer directing many robots; the humanoid positronic setting differs from warehouse fleets.
A two-key activation panel guarding access to a ship's brain relates loosely to computer defences, but no intrusion or tampering is shown.
The quote has only a hesitant mention of the Brain; it hints at a controlling machine but shows no coordination of robots.
Millions of hidden microphones routed to a central calculator that screens speech match automated interception with machine screening; ECHELON screened intercepted satellite traffic by keyword.
An application sent to a big computer to be processed matches machine lookup in function; the quote shows no query matching or speed.
Reading the brains of the recently dead matches extraction of knowledge from brain activity in function; no mechanism is described and the real system reads live viewers.
A pilot's delicate mental control of his ship matches thought-driven machine control in function; the mechanism is unspecified.
An aisle of automated phono-typers matches machines that turn speech into typed text; the quote only names the equipment.
Mechanisms reacting selectively to the electrical impulses of brain cells match the key mechanism of a brain signal interface; the controlled purpose is not shown.
A ship's mind flying the vessel on radar matches a computer steering a craft; the quote gives no calculation of orbits or burns.
An autoscanner on a radar-like device that sounds at the first blip matches machine monitoring of tracked contacts; there is no live position display.
A machine with compartments of synonyms for composing prose matches automatic text composition in function; it is a mechanical word-assembly device.
A line asking whether SRB plates were made up on a man shows only a prediction machine in passing, with no battle analysis described.
Feeding data cards into a computer and keying smoking against incidence shows medical data analysis, but no patient records or diagnosis are involved.
Circuitry traced into insulating blocks with alloy junctions and sprayed conductor threads matches printed micro-circuits; it is a module precursor rather than a chip.
A door beam triggering a metallic recorded voice matches artificial speech in function; the voice generation is not described.
A remark that Russia would give top players computers points loosely at chess computers, but not at a machine that plays.
A machine throwing hypnotized captives' thoughts onto a screen matches thought display in function; the real system decoded speech to text with implants.
Lessons learned from tapes and papers corrected automatically match a machine presenting lessons and grading; tape delivery differs from a computer.
An android with a recorded neurological analogue of its owner matches a robot double of a person in function; no body likeness is described.
Robot calculators producing more plausible thoughts than there are positions gestures at machine-made content, but nothing says it composes texts.
A machine controlled by thoughts, designed by another machine, hints at thought control, but the quote does not describe a central machine directing others.
A chess machine programmed to keep analysing during an adjournment matches a computer playing against a human; no consumer product is implied.
A single character standing in a simulated meadow evokes immersive environments, but the quote shows no many people meeting in one world.
Robot controls doing observers' work at asteroid outposts evoke automation, but the quote does not describe a self-running plant.
A brain built of glass tubing and filled with synthetic fluid is brain-like only in name, with no interconnected units or learning.
Punching a designation and seeing it appear on a translucent screen matches a computer showing data on a display; the CRT radar context differs.
Translating brain waves into pictures matches displaying thoughts on a screen in function; the real work decoded speech to text.
A computer that deduces a saboteur and describes him matches computers identifying suspects; it infers from analysis rather than records.
A robot attuned to thought waves obeys its master, matching thought-controlled machines in function; no mechanism is given.
Scratching on a note plate suggests a reusable writing slate, but the quote says nothing about an electronically rewritable surface.
Liquefied wood-pulp insulation around a computer's nerves that termites could destroy is physical sabotage of a machine, not intrusion into or tampering with its data.
Computers working out how long and how slow to fly matches computing flight profiles for a craft; the relativistic purpose differs from orbital maneuvers.
A mirror-like panel rising from a table to show a menu is a built-in screen, but there is no touch or gesture input.
A subminiaturized brain hidden under paint matches very small electronic circuits in function; it names no solid-state components.
A drive computer finding a way to cut power from its monitor circuit relates to computer control, but the quote has no calculation or navigation.
Directing the station computer by vocoder panel to run the precession equipment matches a station computer controlling attitude; voice control is an extra feature.
Feeding a punched paper strip into the autopilot matches computed courses steering a ship; the computing is not placed aboard in the quote.
A single line about being deep-probed first implies a machine examining a person, with no detail on reading thoughts or images.
A projected index giving call numbers and a tape delivered thirty seconds after punching matches retrieval in seconds; it is lookup by number rather than by content query.
Building an exact replica of a city is a duplicate of a place, with no robot double of a particular person shown in the quote.
An identical electronic copy standing in for its owner matches a robot double of a particular person in function; it is a social stand-in, not an animatronic show figure.
Glinting machines with shadowy arms that appear to stranded humans have no exploring or reporting function in the quote.
Taste buds fitted to a robot's tentacle match machine sensing of taste, but the milestone is a hearing system for spoken digits, so the match is loose.
A duplicate matching hair and fingerprints is a robot copy of a specific man in function; Disney's Lincoln was a show figure and the quote mentions no mind copy.
A line calling something an acquired habit hints at a machine reproducing text, but nothing in the quote shows it composing text.
A cap that reads a person's thoughts and stops lying matches mind-reading in function; the real work reconstructed simple viewed images.
A big ship computer nicknamed Sad Cow is a central computer but nothing shows it running a station's systems.
A mechanical brain solving thousands of successive equations matches big scientific calculation; it names no machine speed or scale.
A console giving orbital figures instantly with a map-projection display matches a computer computing orbits; the shipboard graphical display adds detail.
A screen woman whose voice and face follow impulses from information central is an interface avatar, with no ordinary-language conversation shown.
A terminal obtaining recorded material in print, picture or audio form matches on-demand retrieval; no query method or speed is described.
A desk device that hums and announces a meeting is an automatic voice, with no recognition or spoken command.
A composite mechanical mother summoned on panel screens evokes an interactive voice and image, but there is no conversation in ordinary language.
Typing a corrected ship's path into an electronic brain and feeding the answer tape to the autopilot matches computed courses; the computer is an operator console rather than an orbital computer.
Android duplicates of a man and his wife match robot copies of particular people in function; the quote gives no mechanism and no performance setting.
Conceiving a means to turn the spoken word directly into print matches automatic dictation transcription in function; there is no mechanism.
A gong and mechanical voice announcing a visitor is a speaking device in a building, not a home responding to its occupants.
The quote says orders must now be oral, the opposite of thought commands; it shows no brain-signal link.
Preparing a problem to feed to Compy shows a shipboard computer used for calculation, with nothing on courses or burns.
A device delicate enough to detect rho waves from the brain matches brain-signal reading in function; it does not say what is decoded.
A vast cybernetic machine filling a building, called Central Intelligence, matches a central computer; robot coordination is only implied.
The quote is only a question about what stands behind the listener and describes no display.
A mathematician whose cube has columns of buttons for calculating matches a button-operated calculating device; it has no portable or battery detail.
A ship's computer doing the navigational work and never erring matches a computer plotting a vessel's course; the quote has no detail.
